Commentary.Commentary: We are back for the chase! The Indian players are in a huddle where Rohit Sharma is giving them a last-minute pep talk. Now, they spread out to take their respective field positions. Will Young and Rachin Ravindra are the two openers for New Zealand. Mohammad Shami to start proceedings with the ball. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Right then, India have posted a competitive total, but they’ll need a strong effort to keep the Kiwis in check. There was some turn on offer, which could work in their favor, especially with the extra spinner in their lineup. That said, batting tends to get easier under lights, and New Zealand will be counting on that as they aim to secure their spot as Group A toppers. Stay with us as we get ready for the second essay!

Matt Henry, the man of the moment, is up for a quick chat. He says he is pretty happy with his performance as they have put India under pressure but the batters will have a big job to do. Adds that there was a bit of swing with the new ball and they created pressure with early wickets. Mentions that getting those wickets against a good batting lineup like India has always been good for him. Further adds that the batters of his team just have to put pressure back on the Indian side and keep the scoreboard ticking.

New Zealand, on the other hand, were solid right from the start. Matt Henry and Kyle Jamieson were outstanding with the new ball, striking early to remove three key batters. They faced a brief period where chances were hard to come by but maintained tight lines without offering many freebies. Michael Bracewell and Mitchell Santner were as reliable as ever in the middle overs, with Rachin Ravindra also making valuable contributions. Will O'Rourke got the crucial breakthrough of Shreyas Iyer with a well-directed short ball just as he was starting to accelerate. Their death bowling was exceptional, keeping the scoring in check, and Matt Henry capped it off in style with a brilliant five-wicket haul.

For the first time in this Champions Trophy, India found themselves under pressure in the first Powerplay. They lost three early wickets, with Shubman Gill and Rohit Sharma departing quickly, while Virat Kohli couldn’t make an impact in his 300th ODI, thanks to a stunning catch from Glenn Phillips. However, Shreyas Iyer and Axar Patel led the recovery, steadying the innings with a crucial 98-run stand. Just when Iyer seemed settled, he fell, but not before playing some aggressive shots. He managed 79, leaving the all-rounders to take charge. Hardik Pandya put up a fight with a run-a-ball 45, but the Kiwis kept things tight, never really allowing him to break free.

A brilliant bowling display from the Kiwis! They have managed to keep India under 250, which is no small feat against such a formidable batting lineup. Matt Henry was the standout performer with a superb five-wicket haul, but credit must also go to their sharp fielding and some outstanding catches that have made the difference here.

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK! New Zealand struck at the right time by removing Axar Patel, but they haven't quite managed to tighten the screws. Shreyas Iyer has been swift in punishing loose deliveries, while KL Rahul has settled in nicely. With wickets in hand, India will back themselves to accelerate at the death, but a couple of quick strikes could turn the tide. The Kiwis need to stay patient and keep pushing. The pitch has shown signs of turn, and with India boasting four spinners, chasing won't be easy. However, if it settles under the lights and starts skidding onto the bat, it could be a different story.

Commentary.Commentary: We are done with the national anthems and it's now time for the action to commence. Mitchell Santner and his men disperse from the huddle and take their respective positions on the field. They are followed by the two Indian openers, Shubman Gill and Rohit Sharma. Matt Henry will open the attack for the Kiwis. Henry to the Indian captain first up. A slip in place. And off we go...

The giant flags of the two countries have been rolled out, and it is time for the national anthems. The match officials lead the way as the two teams, along with their mascots, make their way to the centre. It will be India's national anthem first, followed by that of New Zealand.

The Indian captain, Rohit Sharma says they wanted to bat first anyway. Adds that having batted second in the past two games, they wanted to bat first and give their bowlers a chance to challenge themselves under lights. Mentions that they want to do things that are useful to them and try to keep things simple. Says that it is all about bowling in partnerships and their seamers and spinners have complemented each other nicely. Informs Harshit Rana has been rested and Varun Chakaravarthy comes in place of him.

Mitchell Santner, the skipper of New Zealand, says that they are going to bowl first as it looks like a pretty good wicket and they have seen a couple of games here. Tells that they want to put pressure early on with their bowling and then want to chase it. Adds that they know they have to go back to Lahore to play in the semi-final and they want to get the job done here. Informs that Daryl Mitchell comes in place of Devon Conway.

India (Playing XI) - Rohit Sharma (C), Shubman Gill, Virat Kohli, Shreyas Iyer, Axar Patel, KL Rahul (WK), Hardik Pandya, Ravindra Jadeja, Mohammad Shami, Kuldeep Yadav, Varun Chakaravarthy (In for Harshit Rana).

New Zealand (Playing XI) - Rachin Ravindra, Will Young, Kane Williamson, Daryl Mitchell (In for Devon Conway), Tom Latham (WK), Glenn Phillips, Michael Bracewell, Mitchell Santner (C), Matt Henry, Kyle Jamieson, Will O'Rourke.
TOSS - The flip of the coin lands in the favour of Mitchell Santner. New Zealand have elected to BOWL first.

PITCH REPORT - Simon Doull is near the deck. He says that the weather is brilliant, with a high of 24 degrees Celsius and a low of 21 degrees Celsius. Adds that a gentle breeze is blowing across the ground. Mentions that the square boundaries measure 63 metres to one side and 71 meters to the other, while the straight hit is 76 meters. Dinesh Karthik joins Doull for the analysis. Karthik informs that this is a black soil wicket with the soil sourced from Pakistan. Further says that the pitch resembles those used in the last couple of matches, appearing on the drier side. States it offers assistance to spinners during the day but it gets better to bat under the lights. Shares that pacers have had a better strike rate and taken more wickets here in Dubai, whereas spinners have maintained a tighter economy rate.

The venue has so far assisted spinners, which plays into the strengths of both teams as they have world-class spin options. The weather looks perfect, with no threat of rain or dew, meaning the toss won’t be a major factor. Even though both teams have already reached the semi-finals, this match will be a crucial test before the semis against a top-quality opposition. Expect a high-intensity battle as both sides look to fine-tune their game and carry winning momentum into the knockouts. Stay tuned, as the toss and playing XI are coming up soon!

New Zealand, on the other hand, have been one of the most well-balanced teams in this tournament and are strong contenders for the title. One of their biggest strengths is their outstanding fielding, which sets them apart from other teams. The only concern is their most experienced batter, Kane Williamson, hasn’t been at his best, getting out cheaply in both matches. His form will be crucial in the knockout stage, and New Zealand will hope he gets some runs today. Their skipper, Mitchell Santner, will be a key player on this pitch. By using his variations smartly, he has shown why he is regarded as one of the best spinners in the world. Given they are scheduled to travel after this game, the Kiwis too might think about resting some players.

India look like a well-settled and balanced side, with all departments performing well as they showed against Pakistan in their last match. All eyes will be on Virat Kohli, who is set to play his 300th ODI, making this a special occasion for him. He is also back in top form, having scored a century in his last match. Shubman Gill is in sublime touch as well, with two centuries and two half-centuries in his last five ODIs. With India’s semi-final scheduled just a day after this match in Dubai, they might consider resting some key players, especially the bowlers, to keep them fresh. However, the big question is, who will be rested? That mystery will be revealed at the toss.

The ICC Champions Trophy 2025 is hurtling toward its climactic showdown. But first, one last delicious appetizer awaits cricket fans as bitter rivals India and New Zealand prepare to lock horns in what promises to be a Group A thriller. Sure, some might dismiss it as a dead rubber, but don't be fooled. For both powerhouses, this clash represents the perfect dress rehearsal before the high-stakes knockout battles begin. But, more than that, it's a fight about who tops the Group A. Fresh and recharged after nearly a week's breather, Team India returns to familiar territory following their masterclass dismantling of Pakistan. Dubai's exclusive status as Team India's tournament home has certainly sparked whispers in cricket circles. But hey, that's just noise outside the boundary rope. Looking at how their tournament has unfolded, India's batting unit has found a solid rhythm. The pre-tournament concerns about Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli's form have largely been addressed, with Rohit providing energetic starts and Kohli delivering when needed most - highlighted by that composed century against Pakistan. Shubman Gill continues his impressive rise, consistently finding runs against quality bowling. The middle order has shown competence when called upon, with Shreyas Iyer and KL Rahul making valuable contributions in their limited opportunities. Hardik Pandya has been more effective with the ball than bat, claiming timely wickets throughout the group stage. In the bowling department, Shami and Rana have generated good pace and movement, while Kuldeep Yadav has maintained his reputation as a crafty spinner who can turn matches. The bench strength remains ready to step in, though they'll be eager for playing time after waiting in the wings. When it comes to ICC tournaments, the Kiwis consistently elevate their game to championship level. Like their Indian counterparts, New Zealand has dismantled both Pakistan and Bangladesh with clinical efficiency. Their batting has been particularly impressive, producing three centurions in just two matches. Tom Latham and Will Young steadied the ship with match-winning hundreds against Pakistan, while Rachin Ravindra immediately stamped his authority with a spectacular century upon returning to the side. The one missing piece in their batting puzzle is Kane Williamson. The typically reliable stalwart has only managed two single-digit scores thus far in the tournament. Should the maestro rediscover his form before the semifinals, New Zealand's batting lineup would become even more formidable for any opposition to contain. The Kiwis' reputation for athletic fielding is embodied perfectly by Glenn Phillips, whose acrobatic saves and bullet throws have become tournament highlights. He has also stepped up significantly with his all-round abilities. While New Zealand's pace attack has operated with impressive discipline and coordination, it's their spin contingent that could prove decisive against India. The ever-reliable Mitchell Santner continues to strangle run-scoring with his metronomic accuracy, while Michael Bracewell, who has emerged as the leading wicket-taker among spinners with the lowest economy rate, seems to have gone under the radar. His ability to build pressure through those streak dot balls makes him another tactical weapon. Add Phillips' useful off-spin to the mix, and the Kiwis have all the tools to test India batters, who have fairly been vulnerable against spin lately. With the Indian batsmen having faced limited spin bowling in the tournament thus far, and the Dubai pitches showing signs of slowing down, New Zealand's spinners might hold the key to testing their opponents' technique and temperament. Cricketing pundits have installed New Zealand as second favorites to lift the trophy and with good reason. Unlike India's fixed venue advantage, the Kiwis have been required to adapt to varying conditions across four different stadiums throughout their group campaign. Now they fly over a thousand kilometres from Pakistan to Dubai for this final league game. Both teams have won their last five ODIs respectively and this marks their first one-day clash after their previous meet at the Wankhede in the 2023 World Cup semifinal. India also holds an edge with a 5-0 lead in their head-to-heads, but can they extend this streak further? Or will Santner’s troops respond strongly this time around? Another mouth-watering clash awaits to light up the ring of fire in Dubai!
